prompt: There are $2017$ turtles in a room. Every second, two turtles are chosen uniformly at random and combined to form one super-turtle. (Super-turtles are still turtles.) The probability that after $2015$ seconds (meaning when there are only two turtles remaining) there is some turtle that has never been combined with another turtle can be written in the form $\frac pq$ where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $p+q$.

Call a number *unremarkable* if, when written in base 10, no two adjacent digits are equal. For example, $123$ is unremarkable, but $122$ is not. Find the sum of all unremarkable 3-digit numbers. (Note that $012$ and $007$ are not 3-digit numbers.)

There is a box containing $100$ balls, each of which is either orange or black. The box is equally likely to contain any number of black balls between $0$ and $100$, inclusive. A random black ball rolls out of the box. The probability that the next ball to roll out of the box is also black can be written in the form $\frac pq$ where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $p+q$.

The four faces of a tetrahedral die are labelled $0,1,2$, and $3$, and the die has the property that, when it is rolled, the die promptly vanishes, and a number of copies of itself appear equal to the number on the face the die landed on. For example, if it lands on the face labelled $0$, it disappears. If it lands on the face labelled $1$, nothing happens. If it lands on the face labelled $2$ or $3$, there will then be $2$ or $3$ copies of the die, respectively (including the original). Suppose the die and all its copies are continually rolled, and let $p$ be the probability that they will all eventually disappear. Find $\left\lfloor\frac{10}{p}\right\rfloor$.

Greedy Algorithms, Inc. offers the following string-processing service. Each string submitted for processing has a starting price of $1$ dollar. The customer can then ask for any two adjacent characters in the string to be swapped. This may be done an arbitrary number of times, but each swap doubles the price for processing the string. Then the company returns the modified string and charges the customer $2^S$ dollars, where $S$ is the number of swaps executed. If a customer submits all permutations of the string PUMAC for processing and wants all of the strings to be identical after processing, what is the lowest price, in dollars, she could pay?

Jackson begins at $1$ on the number line. At each step, he remains in place with probability $85\%$ and increases his position on the number line by $1$ with probability $15\%$. Let $d_n$ be his position on the number line after $n$ steps, and let $E_n$ be the expected value of $\frac1{d_n}$. Find the least $n$ such that $\frac{1}{E_n}>2017$.

If $N$ is the number of ways to place $16$ jumping rooks on an $8\times8$ chessboard such that each rook attacks exactly two other rooks, find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$. (A jumping rook is said to attack a square if the square is in the same row or in the same column as the rook.)

solutions.title: Reduce to two rooks per line, then recurse
solutions.body:
**Every row and column has exactly two rooks.** A rook in a row with $r$ rooks and a column with $c$ rooks attacks $(r-1)+(c-1)$ rooks, so $(r,c)\in\{(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}$. Let $a$ = number of rows with $3$ rooks and $b$ = number with $1$. Since the row counts sum to $16$, $3a+b+2(8-a-b)=16$, so $a=b$; similarly for columns, $a'=b'$. The $3a$ rooks in 3-rows each lie in a 1-column, and every 1-column's rook is in a 3-row, so $b'=3a$; likewise $b=3a'$. Thus $a=b=3a'=3b'=9a$, so $a=0$: all lines have exactly $2$ rooks.

**Counting $0/1$ matrices with all row and column sums $2$.** Fill the board row by row, tracking how many columns still need $2$ rooks ($x$) and how many need $1$ ($y$). Each row picks two columns: both from the $x$ group ($\binom x2$ ways), both from the $y$ group ($\binom y2$), or one of each ($xy$). The resulting recursion, started at $(x,y)=(8,0)$ with $8$ rows, gives
$$N=187\,530\,840$$
(the known sequence $1,0,1,6,90,2040,67950,3110940,187530840$ for $n=0,\dots,8$).

So $N\bmod1000=840$.

**Answer: 840**

solutions.title: Cycle recursion (official method)
solutions.body:
Join two rooks when they share a row or column; since each rook has one partner in its row and one in its column, the graph splits into even cycles alternating row/column steps. Let $f(n)$ count $n\times n$ placements of $2n$ rooks with two per row and column. Analysing how the cycle through the first row can be built (the official solution places $n$ non-attacking rooks on the diagonal and adds the rest) leads to the recursion
$$f(n)=\binom n2\left(2f(n-1)+(n-1)f(n-2)\right),\qquad f(0)=1,\ f(1)=0.$$
Then $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=6$, $f(4)=90$, $f(5)=2040$, $f(6)=67950$, $f(7)=3110940$, $f(8)=187530840$, giving remainder $840$. (A brute-force check of the $4\times4$ case over all placements of $8$ rooks also gives $90$.)

**Answer: 840**

prompt: Bob chooses a 4-digit binary string uniformly at random, and examines an infinite sequence of uniformly and independently random binary bits. If $N$ is the least number of bits Bob has to examine in order to find his chosen string, then find the expected value of $N$. For example, if Bob's string is $0000$ and the stream of bits begins $101000001\ldots$, then $N=7$.

solutions.title: Expected waiting time via overlaps
solutions.body:
For a fixed pattern $s$ of length $4$ in fair coin flips, the expected waiting time is
$$E[N_s]=\sum_{k:\ s\text{ has a border of length }k}2^k,$$
summing over $k\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that the last $k$ bits of $s$ equal its first $k$ bits ($k=4$ always counts). This is the classic "Conway leading numbers" result; the official solution derives it with generating functions: if $A(z)$ counts strings avoiding $s$ and $B(z)$ counts strings ending with the first occurrence of $s$, then $A(z)+B(z)=1+2zA(z)$ and $z^4A(z)=B(z)\sum_{k\text{ border}}z^{4-k}$, and $E[N_s]=A(\frac12)$.

The $16$ strings fall into four classes:

| strings | borders | $E[N]$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0000,1111$ | $1,2,3,4$ | $2+4+8+16=30$ |
| $0001,0011,0111,1000,1100,1110$ | $4$ | $16$ |
| $0010,0100,0110,1001,1011,1101$ | $1,4$ | $18$ |
| $0101,1010$ | $2,4$ | $20$ |

Average: $\frac{2\cdot30+6\cdot16+6\cdot18+2\cdot20}{16}=\frac{304}{16}=19$.

**Answer: 19**

solutions.title: Markov chain check
solutions.body:
For each pattern, track the longest suffix of the bits seen so far that is a prefix of $s$ (states $0$–$3$; state $4$ = found). With $e_j$ the expected number of further bits from state $j$, $e_j=1+\frac12e_{\delta(j,0)}+\frac12e_{\delta(j,1)}$ and $e_4=0$. For $s=0000$: $e_3=1+\frac12e_0$, $e_2=1+\frac12e_3+\frac12e_0$, ..., giving $e_0=30$. Solving these linear systems for all $16$ patterns (by computer) gives the values $30,16,18,20$ above and an average of exactly $19$.

**Answer: 19**
